title: Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN): Relay Extensions to Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN)
summary: Defines TURN, an extension of STUN that lets a host behind a NAT use a relay server to communicate with peers when direct connection is impossible. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 8656.

plainLanguage.summary:
A network address translator sits between a private network and the Internet, and it rewrites addresses on the way through. Two computers behind two of these cannot always talk to each other directly.

TURN adds a middleman on the public Internet. The computer asks it for an address of its own, and the middleman passes messages between the two computers.

questions: how does a turn relay work with nat
what is a channelbind in turn
subtitle: How a host stuck behind a NAT asks a public server to relay its packets to peers it cannot reach directly.

tldr.problem: Two hosts behind awkward network address translators often cannot reach each other, even after trying to open a direct path. When no direct path exists, the traffic has to go through a third party.
tldr.mechanism: TURN extends STUN so that a client can ask a server for a relayed transport address, send data to peers through the server and receive their replies the same way. Permissions control which peers may reach the client.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5766 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 8656, which is the current TURN specification.

facts.label: Overhead of a Send or Data indication

today: RFC 5766 was a Proposed Standard and it has been obsoleted by RFC 8656, which is the current TURN specification. It was also updated by RFC 8155 and RFC 8553. The text described here covers UDP allocations over IPv4 only; extensions for TCP allocations and for IPv6 were planned but are not part of this document.

sections.title: What TURN Is For
sections.content:
A host behind a NAT (Network Address Translation) may want to exchange packets with other hosts, some of which may also be behind NATs. The hosts involved can use hole punching techniques to try to discover a direct communication path, one that goes from one host to another through the intervening NATs and routers without traversing any relay.

As described in RFC 5128 and RFC 4787, hole punching fails if both hosts are behind NATs that are not well behaved. If both are behind NATs with a mapping behaviour of "address-dependent mapping" or "address- and port-dependent mapping", hole punching generally fails.

When no direct path can be found, an intermediate host has to act as a relay for the packets. That relay typically sits in the public Internet and relays packets between two hosts that both sit behind NATs.

This specification defines the protocol, called TURN, that lets a host behind a NAT, the TURN client, ask another host, the TURN server, to act as a relay. The client can arrange for the server to relay packets to and from certain other hosts, called peers, and can control aspects of how the relaying is done. It does so by obtaining an IP address and port on the server, called the relayed transport address. When a peer sends a packet to that address, the server relays the packet to the client. When the client sends a data packet to the server, the server relays it to the peer using the relayed transport address as the source.

A client using TURN needs some way to tell its peers the relayed transport address, and some way to learn each peer's IP address and port, more precisely each peer's server-reflexive transport address. How this is done is out of the scope of TURN. One way might be for the client and peers to exchange email messages; another is a special-purpose "introduction" or "rendezvous" protocol.

If TURN is used with ICE, the relayed transport address and the addresses of the peers are included in the ICE candidate information that the rendezvous protocol has to carry. For example, with TURN and ICE as part of a multimedia solution using SIP, SIP plays the role of the rendezvous protocol and carries the ICE candidate information inside the body of the SIP messages.

Using a TURN server to reach another host behind a NAT is very likely to work, but it comes at a high cost to the provider of the server, since the server typically needs a high-bandwidth connection to the Internet. It is therefore best to use a TURN server only when a direct path cannot be found. When a client and a peer use ICE to determine the path, ICE tries hole punching first and only uses a TURN server when no direct path can be found.

TURN was originally invented to support multimedia sessions signalled with SIP. Because SIP supports forking, TURN supports multiple peers per relayed transport address, a feature other approaches such as SOCKS do not offer. Care has been taken to make TURN suitable for other kinds of application. TURN was designed as one piece of the larger ICE approach to NAT traversal, and implementors are urged to investigate ICE and seriously consider using it, although it is possible to use TURN without ICE.

TURN is an extension to the STUN (Session Traversal Utilities for NAT) protocol. Most, though not all, TURN messages are STUN-formatted messages, so a reader is expected to be familiar with STUN.
sections.plainLanguage:
When a translator on your network and a translator on your peer's network both hide the real address, neither side can send a first packet that the other will accept.

TURN solves this by putting a third machine in the middle, on the open Internet, and having both sides talk to it.

sections.title: The Pieces and the Addresses
sections.content:
In a typical deployment a TURN client sits on a private network and reaches the public Internet through one or more NATs. A TURN server sits on the public Internet, and one or more peers sit elsewhere, behind NATs or not. The client uses the server to send packets to those peers and to receive packets from them.

Several addresses matter, and the difference between them is the heart of the protocol. A transport address is an IP address and port together. The client talks to the server from its host transport address, and the server's own address for TURN messages is the TURN server transport address, which the client learns by some unspecified means such as configuration and which is typically used by many clients at once. Because the client is behind a NAT, the server sees its packets as coming from a transport address on the NAT itself, the client's server-reflexive transport address; packets sent by the server there are forwarded by the NAT to the client's host transport address. The relayed transport address is the address on the server that peers use to have data relayed to the client. The peer transport address is the peer's address as seen by the server, which for a peer behind a NAT is that peer's server-reflexive address.

The client uses TURN commands to create and manipulate an allocation on the server, a data structure that holds the relayed transport address and other state. An allocation is uniquely identified by its relayed transport address, and each allocation belongs to a single client and has exactly one relayed transport address used only by that allocation, so the server knows which client a packet arriving at that address is meant for. A client may hold several allocations on a server at the same time.

Once an allocation exists, the client sends application data to the server together with an indication of which peer should receive it, and the server relays the data. The data travels inside a TURN message; at the server it is extracted and sent to the peer in a UDP datagram. In the other direction a peer sends a UDP datagram to the relayed transport address, and the server encapsulates it in a TURN message for the client, with an indication of which peer sent it. Because the message always names the peer, one allocation can serve several peers.

TURN always uses UDP between the server and the peer, but the client and server may use UDP, TCP or TLS over TCP. If TCP or TLS is used between client and server, the server converts to and from UDP when relaying to the peer. TCP is supported because some firewalls block UDP entirely, and TLS is supported because it lets the client confirm it is talking to the right server and keeps the TURN control messages confidential. TLS is not required, because its overhead is higher than digest authentication and most application data would end up encrypted twice. The version described here supports only IPv4.

The server is designed to run as an ordinary user-space application without special privileges, so that it can be deployed easily, for example inside a peer-to-peer application so that one peer can offer NAT traversal to another. That choice has consequences for relayed data: the Diffserv field may not be preserved, the TTL field may be reset rather than decremented, the ECN field may be reset, ICMP messages are not relayed, and there is no end-to-end fragmentation because the packet is reassembled at the server.
sections.plainLanguage:
The protocol juggles several addresses. The client has one address inside the private network, the NAT gives it a different one on the outside, and the TURN server hands out a third that peers can aim at.

The server deliberately runs as an ordinary program, without special privileges, so that it is easy to deploy.

sections.title: Allocations, Permissions and Refreshes
sections.content:
To create an allocation the client uses an Allocate transaction. It sends an Allocate request to the server, and the server replies with an Allocate success response containing the allocated relayed transport address. The client can include attributes describing the kind of allocation it wants, such as its lifetime. Because relaying data has security implications, the server requires the client to authenticate itself, typically with STUN's long-term credential mechanism, to show that it is allowed to use the server.

The client must keep the allocation alive. It does so by periodically sending a Refresh request, and TURN deliberately uses a separate Refresh method rather than Allocate so that the client is told if the allocation disappears for some reason. The frequency of the refresh follows the lifetime of the allocation, whose default is 10 minutes. That default was chosen to be long enough that refreshing is not typically a burden on the client while still expiring allocations of clients that quit unexpectedly in a timely manner. The client can ask for a longer lifetime in the Allocate request and change it in a Refresh request, and the server always states the actual lifetime in the response. The client must issue a new Refresh within "lifetime" seconds of the previous Allocate or Refresh. To give an allocation up, the client sends a Refresh with a requested lifetime of zero.

Both sides keep track of a 5-tuple: the client's host transport address, the server transport address and the transport protocol used between them. At the server the client's host transport address is replaced by the client's server-reflexive address. The 5-tuple used in the Allocate request identifies the allocation, and later messages use the same 5-tuple. A second relayed transport address needs a second allocation, made with a different 5-tuple, for example by using a different client address or port.

TURN also has the notion of permissions, which exist to ease the concern of enterprise administrators that TURN could be used to get around corporate firewall rules. Permissions mimic the address-restricted filtering of a NAT that complies with RFC 4787. An allocation can have zero or more permissions, each an IP address and a lifetime. When a UDP datagram arrives on the allocation's relayed transport address, the server first checks the permission list; if the source IP address matches a permission the data is relayed to the client, and otherwise the datagram is silently discarded.

A permission expires after 5 minutes if it is not refreshed, and there is no way to delete one explicitly. That behaviour was chosen to match a NAT that complies with RFC 4787. The client installs or refreshes a permission with either a CreatePermission request, which can install several at once and matters for applications using ICE, or a ChannelBind request. For security, permissions can only be installed or refreshed by transactions that can be authenticated, so Send indications and ChannelData messages never install one. Permissions belong to an allocation, so adding or expiring one in one allocation does not affect any other.
sections.plainLanguage:
The client asks for an address on the server and gets one. It then has to keep that address alive by refreshing it every so often.

Before the server will forward anything to the client, the client must name the peer it expects to hear from. Those names are permissions, and they expire after five minutes unless renewed.

sections.title: Two Ways to Move Data
sections.content:
There are two mechanisms for exchanging application data, and both let a single relayed transport address serve several peers. Both include a way for the client to say which peer should receive data, and a way for the server to say which peer sent it.

The Send mechanism uses Send and Data indications. A Send indication carries an XOR-PEER-ADDRESS attribute with the peer's server-reflexive transport address and a DATA attribute holding the application data. On receiving it, the server extracts the data and sends it to the peer in a UDP datagram, using the allocated relayed address as the source. There is no need to name the relayed transport address, because it is implied by the 5-tuple of the indication. In the other direction, a UDP datagram arriving at the relayed transport address is turned into a Data indication and sent to the client, with the peer's server-reflexive transport address in an XOR-PEER-ADDRESS attribute and the data in a DATA attribute.

Send and Data indications cannot be authenticated, because the long-term credential mechanism of STUN does not support authenticating indications. This is less serious than it looks, because the client-to-server leg is only half of the path to the peer, and applications that want real security should encrypt the data between client and peer themselves. It does mean an attacker can send bogus Send indications that the server will relay to a peer. To partly mitigate that, TURN requires the client to install a permission towards a peer before sending data to it with a Send indication.

The channel mechanism exists for applications such as Voice over IP, where the 36 bytes of overhead that a Send or Data indication adds can substantially increase the bandwidth needed between client and server. The ChannelData message does not use the STUN header at all, but a 4-byte header that carries a channel number. Each channel number in use is bound to a specific peer and is a shorthand for that peer's address.

To bind a channel, the client sends a ChannelBind request with an unbound channel number and the peer's transport address. Once bound, the client can send data for that peer inside a ChannelData message, and the server can relay data back from that peer the same way. Channel bindings last for 10 minutes unless refreshed, which is longer than the permission lifetime, and are refreshed by sending another ChannelBind request. As with permissions, there is no way to delete a binding explicitly; the client waits for it to time out.

Once a channel is bound, the client may freely mix ChannelData messages and Send indications. It might use a Send indication, for example, so that it can use the DONT-FRAGMENT attribute, but the server will always answer a bound peer with a ChannelData message. ChannelData messages can only be used for peers the client has bound a channel to, so data for other peers still uses the Send mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to pass data through the server. The general one names the peer on every message, which costs 36 extra bytes each time. The fast one binds a short number to a peer, so the name does not have to travel.

sections.title: The New STUN Methods and Attributes
sections.content:
TURN defines six new STUN methods. Allocate is 0x003, Refresh is 0x004, Send is 0x006, Data is 0x007, CreatePermission is 0x008 and ChannelBind is 0x009. Allocate, Refresh, CreatePermission and ChannelBind have only request and response semantics; Send and Data have only indication semantics.

The extension also defines new STUN attributes: CHANNEL-NUMBER is 0x000C, LIFETIME is 0x000D, XOR-PEER-ADDRESS is 0x0012, DATA is 0x0013, XOR-RELAYED-ADDRESS is 0x0016, EVEN-PORT is 0x0018, REQUESTED-TRANSPORT is 0x0019, DONT-FRAGMENT is 0x001A and RESERVATION-TOKEN is 0x0022. Two codepoints, 0x0010 and 0x0021, are reserved; they were previously used for BANDWIDTH and TIMER-VAL. Some of these attributes have lengths that are not multiples of 4, and the STUN rules require any such attribute to be followed by one to three padding bytes so that the next attribute starts on a 4-byte boundary.

TURN adds error codes to the STUN set. 401 Unauthorized means the server is not accepting the client's credentials. 437 Allocation Mismatch indicates that the client has referred to an allocation that does not exist, or that belongs to a different 5-tuple. 438 Stale Nonce points the client at the long-term credential procedure. 441 Wrong Credentials means the credentials in a request that is not an Allocate request do not match the ones used to create the allocation. 442 Unsupported Transport Protocol means the Allocate request asked for a transport protocol the server does not support. 486 Allocation Quota Reached means the server cannot currently create another allocation for that client.
sections.plainLanguage: TURN reuses the STUN message format and adds six new kinds of message, nine new attributes and a handful of error codes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC separates attacks from outsiders and from insiders.

For outsiders, it lists the ways an attacker might try to get something it should not have. An attacker might try to obtain an allocation without authorisation, or with the credentials of somebody else. It might mount an offline dictionary attack against the message digest. It might send fake Refresh or CreatePermission requests, or fake Data indications, or impersonate a server and answer the client's Allocate request. It might eavesdrop on the relayed traffic. And it might mount a TURN loop attack, in which a packet is relayed back and forth between two servers. Against these, the RFC's answer is the long-term credential mechanism, which TURN servers and clients must implement, and the requirement that the server demand that all requests from the client be authenticated with it or something equally strong. A client must also protect itself against a server that redirects it elsewhere, and the RFC requires that credentials used in CreatePermission, Refresh and ChannelBind messages match those used to create the allocation, so that spoofed requests from another user are rejected.

Firewall considerations follow. A firewall can block a client behind it from sending packets to, or receiving packets from, ranges of blacklisted addresses by inspecting the source and destination addresses of the packets entering and leaving it. TURN servers are allowed to restrict the range of peer addresses they will relay to in the same way. A malicious client behind a firewall might try to use an allocation to run a server, such as a DNS or FTP server; this is not possible in TURN, because the server never accepts traffic from a peer for which the client has not installed a permission.

Insider attacks are cases where a client has legitimate credentials but breaks the trust that goes with them. These cannot be prevented by cryptographic means and have to be considered in the design. A client might obtain an allocation and flood it, which is mitigated by the recommendation that the server limit the bandwidth it will relay for a given username, so that excess traffic can be discarded immediately. Because each allocation uses a port number on the server's IP address, the number of allocations is finite, and an attacker might try to consume them all, which is prevented by the recommendation that the server limit the number of active allocations for a given username. TURN servers also give a degree of anonymisation, and a client can chain several servers together, so administrators worried about this can keep logs of the actual source address and port of the client, and of every permission it installs, for forensic tracing. Finally, an attacker might send Refresh or CreatePermission requests that appear to come from another user of the server, which the requirement about matching credentials prevents.
sections.plainLanguage:
A TURN server is a public machine that other people can ask to carry their traffic, so the RFC spends a lot of time on abuse.

Most of the defences come down to two rules: every request must carry the credentials of the account that created the allocation, and the server will only forward traffic to a client from a peer the client has explicitly named.
